End your next message to a friend with a real question, so they have something to answer.
Trade favorite photos from this year with a family member.
Take a walk with a coworker instead of a coffee break, and let the conversation wander.
Check how a friend is handling the holidays, the heat, or the cold, whatever the season brings.
Call someone on their birthday instead of posting on their page.
Plan a piece of a friend's ideal weekend with them, after asking what it looks like.
Photograph a sunset, a first snow, or a blooming tree and send it to someone with a note that it made you think of them.
Ask a coworker to tell you about the best boss or teacher they ever had.
Keep a small list of things friends mention, then ask about one the next time you talk.
Offer to split a bulk order, a delivery, or a seasonal chore with a neighbor.
Name an opinion of a friend's that changed your mind, and tell them so.
Swap childhood favorite books with a friend, or ask what they read to their kids, and share yours.
Write a thank-you note to a coach, a teacher, or a boss from long ago and send it.
Turn a hardware store, nursery, or big-box run into a hangout by bringing a friend along for the project.
Invite a friend to a morning walk before work or school, even once.
Ask someone at your place of worship, gym, or club to tell you how they first came there.
Message a friend who is sick to ask what they need, and offer something specific.
Ask your partner or closest friend what they would like more of from you.
Send a friend a note on the last day of the year about one thing you shared in it.
Ask a friend to try a new recipe with you, in one kitchen or two, on a video call.
Tell a coworker you noticed they seemed off this week and ask if they want to talk.
Ask a family member to teach you something they know how to do: a stitch, a repair, a card trick.
Send a photo of a place from your shared past to a sibling or cousin, and ask what they remember.
Ask a friend to meet for breakfast instead of dinner, and see how different the conversation feels.
Talk to the person next to you on a plane, a train, or a bus for at least a few minutes.
Ask a coworker to grab lunch together on a Friday and leave work talk at the door.
Send a friend a reminder of a promise you made each other, and ask if they still want to keep it.
Ask a neighbor to join you for a walk to the polling place, the park, or the farmers market.
Tell a friend the thing you have been meaning to say and keep putting off, in a message or in person.
Ask a family member which relative you remind them of and why.
Time a message to a friend in another time zone so it lands in their morning.
Visit a museum, a garden, or an exhibit with a friend this month.
Reach out to someone from a support group, a class, or a program you once attended.
Ask a coworker what they do to unwind after work.
Tell a friend that you are around and free on a specific evening this week, and see who takes you up on it.
Ask the person who delivers your mail or packages how their route is going.
Remind a friend that you are thinking of them during a season they find hard.
Swap podcast episode recommendations with a friend and talk about them once you have both listened.
Sit near someone at a coffee shop and say one thing, about the weather, the line, the music.
Pick one person from this year of reaching out and tell them what their company has meant to you.

title: Loosening the Grip of Worry
description: For a mind that spends its days rehearsing what could go wrong. Each day gives you one way to set worry down for a while, so it takes up less of your day.
tasks: Set a fifteen-minute "worry window" this evening. When worries appear earlier, write them down and save them for then.
Write down one worry and sort it: something you can act on, or something you cannot. Act on the first kind, breathe through the second.
Notice one "what if" today and answer it with "even if that happened, I would..."
Take a worry and write down the most likely outcome, not the worst one.
Ask yourself: "Is this worry solving anything right now?" If not, put it down for an hour.
Do something with your hands for ten minutes, cooking, gardening, drawing, and let your mind follow.
Write down a worry from last month. Did it come true? What actually happened?
When you catch yourself worrying, name what you can see, hear, and feel right now.
Pick one small step on the thing you are worried about and do it today.
Limit checking the news to two set times today.
Tell someone one worry out loud. Notice how it changes when it is said.
Breathe out for longer than you breathe in, ten times, when a worry spikes.
Write a worry on paper, fold it, and put it in a drawer until tomorrow.
Notice a worry about someone else and ask whether there is something kind you could do for them instead.
Spend ten minutes on something that fully absorbs you, a puzzle, a game, a craft.
Ask: "What would I tell a friend who was worrying about this?" and take your own advice.
Rate a worry from zero to ten in the morning and again at night. Notice the difference.
Replace one "I can't stop thinking about it" with "I am choosing to think about something else for now."
Make a short list of what is going fine today. Worry tends to leave those off.
Delay checking for a reply or result by thirty minutes today and see what happens in the gap.
Write down the thing you are worried about and next to it the date you will actually know the answer.
Do a quick body check: unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders, loosen your hands.
Write down what you would do if the worst case happened, in three steps. Having a plan shrinks it.
Spend fifteen minutes outside and leave the worry indoors.
Notice a worry that is really about wanting certainty. Say, "I can handle not knowing for now."
Choose one worry to stop researching online today.
Say to a worry: "Thanks for trying to protect me. I have got this."
Make a small decision you have been putting off, in under two minutes.
Look at your worry notes from this challenge and count how many worries came true. Let the number speak.
Write down one thing you want to do this week that worry has been talking you out of, and do the first step.
Before you get out of bed, name the one worry waiting for you and tell it, "Not yet, we will meet at seven tonight."
Keep a small notebook in your pocket today and jot each worry as it arrives, without solving any of them until dinner.
Choose a worry that has been circling for days and ask a simple question: "What is the one fact I am missing?" Go find that fact.
Set a timer for five minutes and worry on purpose, as hard as you can. When it rings, stop and make a cup of tea.
Write a worry as a headline, then write the boring version of the story that most likely follows it.
On your commute, count the worries that show up and give each one a number instead of a reply.
Pick the worry that costs you the most sleep and write down who could actually give you an answer. Contact them today.
Move your worry window to your lunch break today and see whether a daytime slot works better than an evening one.
Notice a worry that begins with "I should have" and ask whether there is anything left to do about it now. If not, close the file.
When a worry arrives while you are working, type it into a note, close the note, and return to the task in front of you.
Take one worry about money and turn it into a single number you can check, a balance, a bill, a date. Check it, then stop.
Send the email, make the call, or fill out the form you have been worrying about instead of doing. Ten minutes is enough.
Ask a worry, "What is the smallest version of this problem?" and deal with that version today.
Walk around the block once and let every worry that comes up ride along without answering it.
Write a worry in pencil and, next to it, in pen, one thing you know for certain about the situation.
Tell a worry, "You can come back at the worry window," and say it out loud if you are alone.
Spot a worry about tomorrow and do one small thing tonight that makes tomorrow easier: lay out clothes, pack a bag, set an alarm.
Ask someone you trust to hold a worry for you today. Say, "I just need to hand this to you for the afternoon."
When a worry says "what if it goes wrong," add "and what if it goes fine?" and sit with both for a minute.
Look at a worry and mark it with a letter: A for act, W for wait, L for let go. Do only what the letter says.
Give a persistent worry a name, like a weather system, and note when it passes through today.
Take a photo of the thing you are worried about, a bill, a message, a calendar, and close the app. It is saved; you do not need to hold it.
Write down three worries and cross out the two you cannot do anything about this week.
Choose one thing you keep checking, a tracker, an inbox, a bank app, and check it once today, at a time you pick in advance.
Before a meeting or appointment, write down what you are worried will happen. Afterward, write what did.
Notice the moment a worry turns into a plan. Write the plan down and let the worry retire.
Wash the dishes slowly and let each worry go down the drain with the water.
Write down the question a worry keeps asking and answer it with "I will find out on" and a date, then put the pen down.
Take a worry that is about being late and leave ten minutes earlier instead of thinking about it.
Read a chapter of a book at lunch instead of rehearsing the afternoon.
Write a worry on a sticky note and stick it to the fridge. It stays there, you go about your day.
Pick a worry about your health and book the appointment or make the call that would settle it, rather than reading about it.
Sit outside for five minutes at sunset and say to yourself, "Whatever I am worried about, it will still be there in the morning, and so will I."
Before bed, write tomorrow's to-do list so your worries have somewhere to sleep other than your head.
Ask yourself whether a worry belongs to today, this week, or someday. Only today's worries get your attention now.
Spot an old worry wearing new clothes. Write down the first time you had it.
Call or text the person you are worried about instead of guessing how they are.
Hold a warm drink and, for each sip, name one worry you are choosing to leave alone until later.
Find the smallest fact that would shrink a worry and go find it: a train time, a price, a due date.
Write down what a worry wants you to do and what you would rather do. Do the second one.
Turn a "what if" into a "when," if it is truly likely, and write down the first step you would take.
Ask a coworker how they handle a shared uncertainty. Borrow one of their tricks today.
Spend a full minute noticing what your body does when a worry arrives, then let your shoulders drop.
Give yourself permission to not know something today. Say it plainly: "I do not know yet, and that is allowed."
Take one worry and write the best-case outcome, the worst-case outcome, and the most likely one. Circle the last.
Set a "no worry zone" for one room of your home today. Worries wait at the door.
Try holding a worry in one hand as if it were a small stone. Open your hand and set it on the table.
Listen to a full song with your eyes closed and give the worry that comes up the length of the song, then no more.
Ask a worry, "Whose job is this?" If it is not yours, hand it back in your mind.
Write a worry as a text you would never send, then delete it.
Do the chore you have been avoiding because worrying about it felt easier than starting.
Look up the one thing that would resolve a worry for good, then close the browser and do not open a second tab.
Ask a worry to wait until you have eaten. Have a proper meal, then see whether it is still as loud.
Say to yourself, "I have handled unknown things before," and name one you handled.
Split a big worry into three small questions. Answer only the one you can answer today.
Notice if you are worrying to feel prepared. Then do one actual preparation instead, like writing a list or checking a map.
Choose an evening activity that requires your hands and eyes, a jigsaw, kneading dough, sorting photos, and give worry the night off.
Write down a worry, then write "so what?" underneath, and answer honestly.
Ask a friend to tell you about their week before you tell them about your worry. Notice whether it shrinks while you listen.
Rate how urgent a worry feels, then rate how urgent it actually is. Act on the second number.
Put your phone in another room for one hour this evening and let the worries that need it wait.
Write one sentence about what you will do if the thing you fear happens, then one about what you will do if it does not.
Tackle the paperwork, the renewal, or the appointment that a worry keeps pointing at. Fifteen minutes, then stop.
Take a worry to the shower with you and let it stay there when you step out.
Draw a circle and write inside it what you control about a worry. Write the rest outside the circle. Only work inside.
When a worry is about someone's opinion, ask whether they have ever said it. If not, file it under "guess."
Notice one worry you have carried for over a year. Ask whether it has earned that much of your time.
Plant something, a seed, a bulb, a cutting, and let the waiting be practice for the other things you are waiting on.
Tell a worry, "I will give you five minutes at four o'clock," then keep the appointment and keep it short.
Write down the worry that showed up most this week and one thing you learned about it.
Start the morning by writing a worry on the back of a receipt and leaving it in your coat pocket until you get home.
While the coffee brews, tell yourself which worry gets the first ten minutes tonight and which ones do not make the cut.
On a walk today, every time a worry appears, name a tree, a car, or a shop you pass instead, and keep walking.
Text someone "How are you?" before worrying about whether they are upset with you.
Take one worry about your job and write down the single question you could ask your manager to settle it. Ask it this week.
Open the letter, message, or statement you have been avoiding. Read it once and note what, if anything, needs doing.
Sort today's worries into two columns, "mine" and "not mine," and give the second column back.
Do a ten-minute tidy of one surface and let your mind file a worry away while your hands file the mess.
Give a worry the last word only after you have said, "I will decide about this on Friday."
Swap ten minutes of reading about a worry for ten minutes of a cookbook, a comic, or a field guide.
Before you check your phone this morning, write down what you are afraid it will say. Then look.
Ask an older relative or friend what they used to worry about at your age, and what came of it.
Pick one worry and write a tiny experiment to test it: ask, look, try. Run it before the end of the day.
When a worry comes up at your desk, stand, stretch, refill your water, and sit back down to the task, not the worry.
Write a worry at the top of a page and underneath list the people who would help if it came true.
Schedule a worry for the weekend and write it on the calendar so your weekday self can trust it will be handled.
Notice a worry that gets louder at night. Tell it you will look at it in daylight, when it is usually smaller.
Cook something that needs stirring and let the stirring be the only thing you have to keep track of.
Make a list of what you would need to know to stop worrying about one thing. Cross off what is unknowable.
Take a worry about a conversation and write your opening sentence. Having the first line makes the rest easier.
Ask yourself what a calm person who knew all the facts would do about this worry today, then do that one thing.
Turn a worry into a checklist of three items. Check the first one off before lunch.
Sit on a bench outside for ten minutes and let the worries pass like traffic. You are not the road.
Write one worry in the past tense, as if it is already over, and see how you feel reading it.
Notice how a worry sounds when you say it slowly, out loud, in an empty room.
Delay reading the news until after breakfast and see whether the morning goes any differently.
Draw a quick map of a worry: the fear in the middle, the facts around it. Look at how much of the page is fact.
Pay one bill, renew one thing, or cancel one subscription that a worry keeps tapping you about.
Spend five minutes at the end of work writing down what you are leaving unfinished, so it does not come home with you.
Compare a worry with the last three times you had it. Write down how those three ended.
Water the plants and, while you do, decide which worry is getting no water from you today.
Look at your calendar and find the date by which one worry will resolve itself. Write "answer arrives" on that day.
Say "maybe" to a worry instead of "yes" or "no," then get on with your afternoon.
Set a two-minute timer and clear your desk, your bag, or your car. A cleared space asks less of a worried mind.
Ask a partner, friend, or roommate to be your "worry parking attendant" tonight. Hand them the ticket and pick it up tomorrow.
Choose one worry and find out its actual deadline. Most have one further away than the mind claims.
Give yourself a bedtime rule: worries after lights out go on the pad by the bed, not into your head.
Notice when a worry is really about being tired. Go to bed half an hour earlier instead of thinking about it.
Make the phone call you have been dreading, and time how long it actually takes.
Before a trip, write a packing list instead of running through everything that could go wrong on the way.
Jot down a worry and, beside it, who else is carrying it. Share the load with them today, even in a sentence.
Take one worry and imagine explaining it to a ten-year-old. Notice which parts you cannot make sound serious.
Put a chair by a window and give a worry ten minutes of your full attention there. When you stand up, it stays in the chair.
Sweep the porch, the steps, or the hallway, and let the rhythm carry a worry out with the dust.
Write down what you will do first thing tomorrow about a worry, then close the notebook for the night.
Spend your lunch break away from screens and give each worry that comes along a nod, but not a seat.
Ask a worry, "Is there a phone number, a form, or a person that would settle this?" and start there.
Note one worry that vanished on its own this month without your help. Let that count as evidence.
Fold laundry and, with each item, set down one small worry you have been carrying since morning.
Name the three things that are most likely to happen tomorrow. Notice how ordinary they are.
Pick a worry that is about a decision and give yourself a deadline to decide. Write the deadline where you will see it.
Wear something comfortable today and notice whether a relaxed body makes worry a little quieter.
Turn off notifications for one app that feeds a worry, just for today, and see what changes.
Take a worry to a friend and ask only one thing: "Have you ever had this one?"
Write down what you are worried about in one sentence, and what you are actually going to do about it in one sentence. Do the second.
Before you fall asleep, list three things that went fine today that you worried about this morning.
Go for a bike ride, a swim, or a long walk and leave your phone behind for the length of it.
Take the first step on a project a worry has been guarding: open the file, buy the paint, email the person.
Say to a worry, "You are a guess," and write down what would make it a fact.
Choose a worry that has a yes or no answer and ask the question today, even if the answer might be no.
Watch clouds, a fire, or a fish tank for five minutes and let a worry drift by at the same speed.
Practice saying "I will find out when I find out" to one worry that cannot be answered today.
Spend the last ten minutes of your workday writing tomorrow's plan, so the evening belongs to you.
Set a limit of one search on a worrying topic today. After that, the browser stays closed.
Write down a worry that is really a wish for someone to be okay. Do one kind thing for them today instead.
Take a worry and imagine it a year from now. Write down whether you think you will remember it.
Fix the small thing that a worry keeps pointing at: the loose handle, the flat tire, the unread form.
Try worrying in the third person, "she is worried that," and notice whether it loosens the grip.
Take a nap, a stretch, or a snack before deciding whether a worry deserves attention. Bodies exaggerate when tired.
Book the thing you have been putting off, the dentist, the oil change, the checkup, and let the booking do the worrying.
Open the blinds first thing and let the morning light in before you let the first worry in.
On a cold morning, warm your hands on a mug and decide which worry is allowed to come to work with you. Only one.
Write a worry on the steamed-up bathroom mirror and watch it fade as the room clears.
Rake leaves, shovel snow, or pull weeds for fifteen minutes and let the effort do what the worrying was pretending to do.
Ask yourself at noon: "Which worry has had the most airtime today?" Give it five minutes, then change the channel.
Write down one worry about a child, a parent, or a pet, and one practical thing you can do for them this week.
Take a worry about being judged and write down the last time someone actually judged you for it. Look at how long ago it was.
Text a friend a photo of something ordinary instead of a message about what you are worried about.
Give a worry a shelf. Say, "This goes on the shelf until Saturday," and put it there each time it climbs down.
Set out tomorrow's breakfast tonight, so one small unknown is already known.
Try a new route to work or the store and let the unfamiliar streets take the attention a worry usually gets.
Ask a worry whether it is about the past, the present, or the future. Only present ones get a response today.
Check one worry against a calendar: is there actually a date for this, or has your mind invented urgency?
Write down the most boring possible explanation for something that is worrying you. Boring is often right.
Do one thing at a time this afternoon and notice whether a worry has less room when you are not juggling.
Say "not now" to a worry three times today and follow through each time by turning to a task.
Write a worry a short letter: "Dear worry, I have heard you. I will review your case at seven." Sign it.
Take a long, slow walk after dinner and give a worry until the first street corner. After that, it walks in silence.
Before a doctor's appointment or a review, write your three questions. Prepared people worry less on the drive.
Spend ten minutes on a hobby that has nothing to do with anything you are worried about.
Leave the worry about what to cook by choosing tonight's dinner now, in one minute, and moving on.
Take a worry about a friend's silence and send a light message. Most silences are busy, not angry.
Write down which worry you would keep if you could only keep one. Let the others go for the day.
Turn a worry into a question you can ask a professional, a plumber, a pharmacist, a bank, and ask it today.
Pick a worry and find out what would happen if you simply did nothing about it for a week.
Say out loud what you would be doing right now if you were not worrying. Do ten minutes of that.
Try a "worry walk" this weekend: walk and worry for the first half, walk and notice for the second half.
Write down three worries and, next to each, whether it has a form, a call, or a wait attached. Do the forms.
Choose a worry about an outcome and write down what you will do the day after, whichever way it goes.
Notice when a worry pulls you to reread a message. Read it once more, then archive it.
Sit at the kitchen table for five minutes with a worry and a piece of fruit. Eat the fruit. Leave the worry.
Sing or hum on the drive home and let a worry find out it cannot compete with a chorus.
Set a rule for today: worries are allowed, but only in writing.
Give one worry a nickname and say, "Oh, it is you again," when it appears.
Ask a worry, "What would I do differently today if I already knew the answer?" and do that.
Take one worry about the future and write what is true about it today. Only today.
Spend an hour offline this evening and let the worries that need a screen wait for tomorrow.
Choose a repeating worry and count how many times it shows up before lunch. Then let the count be enough.
Write down what you would pay to have a worry answered, then notice you already have the time to find out for free.
Notice a worry about a deadline and check the deadline. If it is real, do fifteen minutes on it. If it is not, note the real date.
Take a worry about money and make one small move: transfer a few dollars, cancel a trial, check a rate.
Spend a few minutes with a pet, a plant, or a view, and let a worry watch from the sidelines.
Ask a worry, "Are you helping me prepare or just helping me feel busy?" and act on the honest answer.
Make a note of one thing you were worried about at this time last year. Write down how it turned out.
Stand in the doorway before leaving home and say, "Whatever happens today, I will handle it at the time."
When a worry says "everyone will notice," ask who "everyone" is. Write down the actual names, if any.
Bake something simple and let the timer do the waiting so you do not have to.
Write down a worry about someone else's choice and remind yourself which choices are theirs to make.
Pick a task you have been circling and give it the first twenty minutes of your morning, before any worry can argue.
Change one worrying thought into a scheduling decision: "I will think about this at three, for ten minutes."
Take a worry about the weather, the traffic, or the delay and write what you will do if it happens. Then check the forecast once.
Read a poem or a short story before bed rather than your worry list.
Try a slow evening stretch and, with each breath out, let one worry loosen its hold.
Go through your worry notes and highlight the ones that were answered by simply waiting.
Ask someone to tell you the most likely outcome of a worry. Outsiders are often better at odds.
Notice a worry that comes with a "should" and change it to "I am choosing to," or drop it.
Write on a card, "I do not have to solve this today," and carry it in your wallet.
Spend the first five minutes at your desk on one concrete task, not on checking anything.
Take one worry to the gym, the pool, or a trail and let it try to keep up.
Say to a worry, "I will believe you when you bring evidence," and get on with your day.
Draft the difficult message you have been worrying about, then leave it in drafts until tomorrow. Drafting is doing.
Sort your worries by size, pebble, rock, boulder, and carry only the pebbles today.
Look around the room and name three things that are working: the lights, the heat, the door that locks.
Ask a worry whether it would still be a worry if you had slept nine hours. If not, plan for the sleep.
Spend ten minutes learning something new and unrelated, a word, a knot, a chord, and give the worry no room to sit.
Write down a worry as a to-do instead: not "what if the car breaks down" but "book the service."
Give yourself a "done for today" time and, when it arrives, tell any worry that shows up that the office is closed.
Wake up and, before anything else, write down the worry that arrived overnight. Then decide whether it gets any daylight.
Pack your lunch or your bag the night before and take one "did I forget" off tomorrow morning's list.
Take a worry about a test result, a grade, or a verdict and write down the two most likely responses you would have. Pick which one you would rather practice.
Spend five minutes in a park, a yard, or a parking lot with trees, and give your worry to the wind for that long.
Ask a worry to show you its receipt. What has it ever bought you? Write the honest answer.
Tell a coworker one small thing you are unsure about and ask what they would do. Sharing the unknown halves it.
Hand-write a worry in the largest letters you can, then in the smallest. Notice which size feels truer.
Delete one app, bookmark, or feed that keeps handing you fresh things to worry about.
Do the task you are worried about badly on purpose, just a first draft, and see whether the worry had anything left to say.
Take a worry about a relationship and say one honest sentence to the person instead of guessing for another day.
Give a worry a color and picture it fading a shade every time you choose to do something else.
Write down what you would tell your younger self about the thing you are worried about now.
Set a "check-in" not a "check": look at the thing you are worried about once, note the status, and close it.
Make your bed slowly and let the flattened sheets be your signal that today's worry is smoothed out too.
Notice a worry that sounds like a family member's voice. Ask whether it is yours to keep.
Try answering a worry with "we will see," and let the phrase be a complete sentence.
Do a chore outdoors, washing the car, sweeping the walk, clearing gutters, and let the air take some of the worry.
Take one worry and write down what "good enough" would look like. Aim for that, not for certainty.
Let a worry wait until you have finished a page, a task, or a walk. Then ask it to wait again.
Spend the ride home listening to a podcast about something you know nothing about.
Write down the person you would call if the thing you worry about happened. Notice you already have a first step.
Notice a worry that is asking you to control someone else. Choose one thing you can do for yourself instead.
Finish something small today, a form, a drawer, a reply, and let "finished" be louder than "what if."
Take a worry and ask, "What is the next right thing?" Do only the next one.
Sit in the car for one minute before going inside and leave the day's worries in the passenger seat.
Write a worry as a weather report: "Cloudy with a chance of overthinking." Then check what the sky is actually doing.
Choose one worry that always comes with a reread. Today, read the message once and answer it instead.
Ask yourself what you would do this weekend if you were not worrying. Put one of those things on the calendar.
Eat lunch away from your desk and let the worry stay with the keyboard.
Take a worry about a mistake you made and write the sentence you would say to apologize or fix it. Say it if it fits.
Write the date on a worry, and set a reminder to reread it in a month.
Notice a worry that starts with "what will they think" and answer, "They are mostly thinking about themselves."
Give a worry exactly three sentences on paper, no more. Fold the page in half when you reach the third.
Do something slightly brave that a worry has been steering you away from: speak first, sit in the front row, ask the question.
Buy the groceries, fill the tank, or top up the account you keep worrying about running out.
Spend a few minutes on a windowsill, a stoop, or a balcony and give a worry the same attention you give the pigeons.
Put a price on finding out: ask a worry what it would cost to know. If it is a phone call, pay it today.
Write a worry on your hand in the morning and wash it off after lunch, whether or not it has been solved.
Notice a worry that peaks on Sunday evening. Put one nice thing in Monday morning so it has less to say.
Try saying "I am worried, and I am also going to make dinner," and then make dinner.
Choose the worry that interrupts you most at work and give it a scheduled slot in your calendar, with an end time.
Do a sudoku, a crossword, or a word game over coffee and let a worry sit out one round.
Take a worry about aging, yours or someone else's, and do one small act of care today instead of forecasting.
List what worries you and what you are grateful for, side by side. Read the right column twice.
Ask a worry, "Would I want a friend to spend their evening on this?" If not, spend yours on something else.
Spend ten minutes clearing out a bag, a drawer, or an inbox and notice which worries were attached to old things.
Say "that is a tomorrow problem" out loud to one worry, and mean it.
Take a worry about someone's safety and send a simple "thinking of you." Then trust them with their own day.
Practice waiting: stand in the longest checkout line on purpose and notice the worry you would usually fill it with.
Write a worry, then write what you would need to see in order to be ninety percent sure it will not happen. Go check for that.
Give a worry a run: jog, march, or walk fast for ten minutes and see how much of it is left when you stop.
Before a family gathering, write down the one thing you are worried someone will say. Then write your calm reply.
Take a worry about being enough and list three things you did today that were, in fact, enough.
Turn a "what if I fail" into "what if I try," and take the first step within the hour.
Sit with your back to your desk for two minutes and give your eyes a worry-free view.
Write down one worry you have never said out loud, then say it to one person you trust today.
Notice a worry that has a "should have by now" attached. Cross out "by now."
Choose one worry to hand to your future self. Write, "Future me will handle this on" and a date. Then trust them.
Take a worry about the house and do one repair, one call, or one measurement toward it today.
Spend the first hour of a day off without checking anything. Let the worries find out you are not available.
Write a worry as a "maybe" and its opposite as a "maybe" too. Hold both for the day.
Ask a worry, "Is this a two-minute thing?" If it is, do it now and let the worry go with it.
Take a worry about the future of your work and update one thing today: a resume line, a skill, a contact.
Do one small favor for a neighbor and notice whether your worry had to wait while you did it.
Write "answer pending" on a worry and stop trying to write the answer yourself.
Set the table, light a candle, or put on music for dinner and give the evening a shape that worry has to fit around.
Notice one worry that dissolves when you say it to another person. Keep a list of those.
Say to yourself in the mirror, "I can worry later, and I probably will not need to," and leave the bathroom.
Start the day with a stretch by the window and tell the first worry you spot, "Later, and in writing."
Take a worry about a trip, a move, or a change and do one concrete thing toward it: a list, a booking, a box.
Try describing a worry as if it were a small animal you found on the path. Notice it, step around it, keep walking.
Write down a worry that you have already solved once. Reread your old solution and reuse it.
Ask a worry to name a date. If it cannot, it does not get a spot on your calendar today.
Spend fifteen minutes doing something generous, a note, a delivery, a call, and let worry find the door locked.
Notice one worry that is about wanting to be liked. Do something you like instead, for ten minutes.
Wash your face with cold water and say, "That is enough of that one," to the worry you have been holding since breakfast.
Choose a worry to put in a jar, literally, on a slip of paper. Empty the jar at the end of the season and read what came true.
Revisit a conversation that still worries you and write what you would say if you got a second chance. Then decide if you need one.
Try worrying only while standing today. Sit down, and the worry has to wait.
Give one worry a "consult": ask an expert, read one reliable page, and then stop collecting opinions.
Write down what you will not do about a worry today, and let "not doing" be a decision rather than an accident.
Take a worry to a body of water, a river, a pond, a fountain, and let the water carry your attention for five minutes.
Ask yourself what a worry wants you to avoid, then do a tiny version of that thing.
Send the thank-you, the RSVP, or the follow-up you have been worrying about being late with. Late is better than never, and it is done.
Take a worry about a child's future and do one thing with them today that has nothing to do with the future.
Try a "worry swap" with a friend: each of you names one, and you talk about the other person's, not your own.
Write down one worry as a question to a stranger on a bus. Notice how odd it sounds when it leaves your head.
Do a slow loop of your home and touch three things that are fine: the locked door, the full fridge, the working faucet.
Give a worry a "seat" in the room, a chair or a cushion, and speak to it there, briefly, then leave the room.
Ask a worry what it would say if it were kind. Write that version down and read it instead.
Make one decision today without checking with anyone, and let the worry about being wrong come along for the ride.
Water a garden, a lawn, or a windowsill and let a worry wait for the can to empty.
If a friend's health worries you, ask them directly how they are, rather than reading between lines.
Write on a slip of paper, "This will be answered by" and a date. Tape it to the mirror and stop rewriting the ending.
Spend a rainy hour indoors with a project that needs your hands more than your head.
Notice a worry that arrives in the shower or the car, places you cannot act. Say, "I will look at you when I have hands and a desk."
Take a worry about a purchase and sleep on it. If it still matters tomorrow, decide then.
Try one hour of "single-tasking" this afternoon and notice whether worry has fewer gaps to slip into.
Take a worry about the past and write down the one thing you would do differently. Then write, "I did not know that then."
Set a timer for two minutes and list everything that is not wrong right now. Keep the list nearby.
Give a worry to a walk with a dog, a friend, or a podcast, and see how much of it makes it home.
Write down one worry that a good night's sleep would shrink. Go to bed at a reasonable hour tonight and check in the morning.
Ask a worry to prove it with one fact. Give it thirty seconds. If nothing comes, move on.
Choose a worry about a gathering and write your exit plan. Knowing you can leave makes staying easier.
Take a worry about a bill and call the company. Most have a plan, a date, or an answer.
Try a "worry-free hour" with a friend or partner and agree to talk about anything else.
Plan tonight's replacement for worrying, in writing. Be specific: a show, a bath, a chapter, a call.
Take a worry about a loud world and turn the volume down, literally, for an hour: no radio, no notifications, no news.
Do the thing a worry says is too hard for five minutes, then decide whether to keep going.
Write down the biggest worry of the month and one small thing you are proud of doing about it.
Try telling a worry, "You are welcome to stay, but I am going to the store," and go to the store.
Take a worry about being behind and write down where you actually are. Compare with the finish line, not with someone else.
Ask a worry, "Who is this really for?" If it is for someone else, do them a favor rather than a forecast.
Take a worry outside on a clear night and look up for a full minute. Notice how far away it feels from up there.
Choose the worry you would most like to retire and write its retirement date. Mark the day with something small.
Write your worries on a whiteboard or a big page and erase one each time you act on it, wait on it, or let it go.
Say "not today" to one worry and "yes, today" to one task. Do the task.
Spend the last five minutes of the day writing what tomorrow's first step is. Nothing else goes on the page.
Take a worry about an apology you owe and make it, simply, in one sentence.
Sit with a warm meal and give a worry the length of the meal. Then clear the table, and the worry with it.
Try a "sounds like" for one worry: "That sounds like the one about not being ready." Naming the pattern loosens it.
Take one worry and imagine handing it to a very calm person. Write what they would do first, then do that.
Go through your worry notes from this challenge and pick the one tool you will keep using after it ends.
Let the last worry of the day be written, not thought. Then close the notebook and turn out the light.
Write down what a year of setting worry down has taught you, in three sentences, and keep the page where you will find it again.
Spend five minutes at a window or a doorway watching people or weather go by, and let a worry go by with them.
Take a worry about the season ahead, the holidays, the heat, the dark, and plan one thing you will enjoy in it.
Try listing what you know for certain about a worry. Read the list twice, then go do the next ordinary thing.

title: Holding Your Boundaries
description: For people who say yes when they mean no, or feel used up by everyone else's needs. Each day is one small practice in noticing your limits and stating them plainly and kindly.
tasks: Write down one thing you agreed to recently that you did not want to do.
Say "Let me check and get back to you" to one request today instead of answering right away.
Notice one moment today when your body tightened. That is often a boundary being crossed.
Practice saying "No, I can't do that" out loud, alone, five times.
Turn down one small thing today, an extra task, a call, a favor, with one sentence and no apology.
Decide on a time to stop working today and stop at that time.
Write down three things you need more of: time, quiet, help, rest, and one way to get one of them.
Tell someone what you would prefer, instead of going along with their plan.
Leave one message unanswered until tomorrow. Nothing will break.
Say "I am not available then, but I could do Thursday" to one request.
Notice one time you over-explained yourself today and practice a shorter version.
Set your phone to do not disturb for one hour and tell the people who might need to know.
Write down one boundary you wish you had held recently and how you would say it next time.
Ask for what you need today in one clear sentence: "I need some quiet for an hour."
Let someone else handle something you would normally take over.
Say "That does not work for me" once today and leave it there.
Take your full break at work or school today, away from your desk if you can.
Notice a guilty feeling after saying no and remind yourself: guilt is not proof you did something wrong.
Decide on one topic you will not discuss with a particular person, and change the subject if it comes up.
Write down the difference between what someone wants from you and what you owe them.
Give yourself an hour today that no one else gets to schedule.
Practice a gentle exit line: "I need to go now, let's talk soon."
Notice one person who respects your boundaries easily and thank them for it.
Say "I will think about it" to something you are tempted to agree to on the spot.
Stop doing one thing today that you only do to avoid someone's disappointment.
Tell someone how you would like to be spoken to, calmly, in one sentence.
Set a limit on one thing that drains you, screen time, a group chat, and hold it today.
Write down what you are afraid will happen if you hold a boundary. Then write what usually actually happens.
Hold one boundary today and afterward write down how your body felt.
Reread your notes from this challenge and pick the one boundary that matters most. Write it as a sentence you can say.
Before you answer any request this morning, take one full breath and ask yourself whether you actually have the time.
Write down the three people you find it hardest to say no to. Next to each name, note why.
Practice saying "I would rather not" in the mirror until it sounds ordinary rather than dramatic.
Decline one meeting invitation today that has no clear reason for you to be there.
Notice one request today that arrived as a statement rather than a question, and answer it as if it were a question.
End a phone call at the time you said you would, even if the other person is still talking.
Say "I can do half of that" to one task today instead of taking all of it.
Pick one chore at home that is not yours and leave it undone for someone else to do.
Tell a friend one thing you would like to change about how your time together usually goes.
Write down a boundary you hold easily with strangers and ask why it is harder with people you love.
Choose a cutoff time for reading work email tonight and close the app at that time.
Ask a coworker to send their request in writing so you can consider it before you respond.
Say "I do not lend that" or "I do not share that" about one possession today, kindly and without a story.
Notice when you nod along in a conversation today and see if you can stay still instead.
Mute one group chat for the rest of the day and see what changes.
Tell one person what time you need to leave before an event begins, so leaving is not a surprise.
Write down what a "soft no" sounds like for you and what a "clear no" sounds like. Use the clear one once.
Let a phone call from a family member go to voicemail and call back when you are ready.
Refuse one favor today that you would have said yes to a month ago.
Say "I am going to pass" to one invitation and resist the urge to add a reason.
Ask yourself before bed: what did I give away today that I did not want to give?
Decide how many minutes you will spend on one draining errand and stop when the minutes are up.
Tell your partner or housemate one thing you need them to stop doing in shared space.
Practice the sentence "That is not something I can take on right now" until it fits in your mouth.
Turn off notifications for one app that pulls at you and leave them off through dinner.
Say what you want to eat when someone asks, rather than "whatever you like."
Write down one way you make yourself smaller to keep someone comfortable, and skip it once today.
Ask for the deadline before you agree to a task at work, then decide whether it is realistic.
Sit down to eat lunch today without answering messages, and tell anyone waiting that you will reply afterward.
Give a short, honest answer when someone asks how you are, instead of the automatic "fine."
Notice a request today that came with flattery attached and separate the compliment from the ask.
Close your laptop at the end of the workday and put it somewhere out of sight.
Say "Please ask me first next time" to someone who assumed you would be available.
Write a two-sentence reply to a long message instead of matching its length.
Tell a friend you need to reschedule because you are tired, without dressing up the reason.
Choose one thing you will not volunteer for this month and write it down.
Notice one person who tends to talk over you and finish your sentence anyway.
Say "I need to think about whether I have room for that" to one request and mean it.
Set a limit on how late you will stay at a social event tonight and leave then.
Write down three things you are responsible for and three things that are not yours to carry.
Ask a family member to knock before entering your room, and say why it matters to you.
Turn down an extra shift or extra project today if you were already at capacity.
Practice saying "No thank you" without lowering your voice or looking away.
Notice how you feel in the first minute after saying no and write one word for it.
Tell someone who keeps rescheduling on you what you need from them going forward.
Decline to explain a decision when someone pushes for reasons you do not owe them.
Set a rule about what hours you will answer texts from a particular person and follow it tonight.
Say "I am not the right person for that" to one request that lands on you by habit.
Write down one thing you are tired of being the default for, and name who else could do it.
Ask a colleague to take a turn with a task you usually handle, and let them do it their way.
Say "I will let you know by Friday" instead of answering a big ask on the spot.
Notice a moment today when you laughed at something that bothered you, and say what you felt instead.
Put your phone in another room for the first hour of the morning.
Tell someone who asks for advice that you would rather just listen today.
Write down the last time you said yes out of fear of seeming rude. What would you say now?
Leave a conversation that has turned into complaining by saying you need a break.
Pick one social obligation on your calendar you dread and decide honestly whether to keep it.
Say "That is your decision to make" when someone tries to hand you a choice that belongs to them.
Ask to be removed from one email thread or mailing list that adds nothing to your day.
Practice a gentle interruption today: "I want to add something before we move on."
Tell a friend or relative that you will not be answering messages during your vacation.
Write down one thing you keep doing for someone that they could do themselves.
Notice the pull to fix a problem someone mentioned today, and let it stay theirs.
Say "I need a minute" and take it, instead of answering while overwhelmed.
Tell someone the truth about why you did not come, rather than a polite excuse.
Ask a neighbor or coworker to give you a heads-up before dropping by.
Decide how much of your weekend belongs to you and block it off before anyone else claims it.
Write the boundary you find hardest to say as a text message, then decide whether to send it.
Turn down a request from someone you admire, and notice that admiration does not require a yes.
Say "I am at capacity" to one person today, and let the phrase stand on its own.
Start the morning by writing one sentence about what you will protect today: an hour, a task, a mood.
Tell a coworker who messages after hours that you will see it in the morning, then do not open it.
Practice saying "I hear you, and my answer is still no" in a calm voice.
Notice one moment today when you said "sorry" for taking up space and replace it with "thank you for waiting."
Ask someone who borrowed something to return it by a specific day.
Decline a plan this weekend if you were only going to avoid letting someone down.
Write down what you would do with an extra free evening this week, then clear one.
Say "I would like to finish my thought" the next time you are cut off.
Set a specific end time for helping a friend with a task, and tell them when you start.
Tell your family which holiday traditions you will join this year and which you will skip.
Notice one favor you are about to offer before anyone asks, and hold it back to see if it is needed.
Write a script for declining an invitation from someone who takes no personally, and keep it in your phone.
Refuse to be put on speakerphone or added to a call you did not agree to join.
Pick one recurring commitment and ask yourself whether you would sign up for it again today.
Tell a friend who vents at length that you have twenty minutes and then need to go.
Say "I am choosing not to" instead of "I can't" once today and notice the difference.
Turn off your camera or leave a video call when your part is done.
Write down what someone's silence after your no is telling you, and what it is not telling you.
Let a dish, a text, or a small errand wait until you have eaten.
Ask your partner or a close friend what boundary of yours they notice you not holding.
Say no to a second helping, a second drink, or a second round when you have had enough, and leave it at that.
Decide what you will and will not talk about at a family meal, and stick with it.
Notice a moment when someone changes the subject away from what you asked for. Ask again.
Tell a relative that you will not be discussing your relationship, your job, or your plans tonight.
Write a boundary for your workspace at home: hours, noise, interruptions, and share it with anyone it affects.
Say "I am not comfortable with that" about one thing today, without softening it afterward.
Take the last slice, the good seat, or the first turn once today without checking that it is okay.
Decline to answer a personal question from a coworker by saying "I keep that private."
Ask a friend to text before calling so you can pick a good time.
Write down one place where "being helpful" has turned into "being used," and one line to change it.
Say what you actually think in one meeting today, even if it is not the popular view.
Notice how many times you check whether someone is upset with you today, and skip one check.
Tell a friend who always picks the restaurant that you would like to choose this time.
Set a boundary with yourself: one thing you will not do for others after nine tonight.
Say "Not tonight" to one request and let the evening be yours.
Practice a boundary around money: "I am not able to lend that" or "I split checks evenly."
Refuse to be rushed into a decision by saying "If you need an answer now, the answer is no."
Ask to move a deadline that was set without asking you.
Notice someone else's hurry today and check whether it needs to become yours.
Write down what you would say to a friend who was being asked what you are being asked.
Tell the person who expects an instant reply that you answer messages twice a day.
Say "I will pass this time" to a group activity you do not enjoy and stay home without guilt.
Decide who gets to give you feedback on your appearance, and stop taking it from everyone else.
Leave a family group chat conversation that turns tense by saying you will pick it up later.
Ask a coworker to stop copying you on emails that do not need your input.
Say no to a hug, a handshake, or a kiss on the cheek if you do not want one today.
Write down the tasks at work that are yours and the ones you have absorbed, then hand one back.
Tell a friend who is often late that you will wait fifteen minutes and then go ahead.
Notice one request today that assumed you had nothing else going on, and correct the assumption.
Say "Let me finish this first" when someone interrupts your work.
Decline to babysit, pet-sit, or house-sit once when you would rather have the time.
Ask your manager which of two tasks matters more, rather than doing both late tonight.
Turn down a road trip, a dinner, or a weekend plan by text with two sentences and no apology.
Write down what you tell yourself you owe your parents, and check which items are true.
Tell someone who keeps offering unsolicited advice that you are not looking for suggestions right now.
Set an alarm for the end of your workday and treat it as seriously as the start.
Say "I have plans" when the plan is rest, and let that be a full answer.
Notice the difference between someone being disappointed and someone being harmed, and let the disappointment be.
Ask for a break in a long conversation instead of pushing through.
Practice saying "That is between you two" when someone tries to pull you into their argument.
Write a short list of what you will do when someone ignores a boundary: repeat it, step back, or leave.
Tell a friend you cannot be their emergency contact for every small crisis, and suggest who else could help.
Decide what time you will stop checking the news tonight and hold it.
Say no to a favor for a neighbor if it would cost you the one free hour you had.
Refuse to apologize for something that was not your fault today, even if silence feels awkward.
Jot down what you fear people will think of you if you hold a limit, then write what you think of people who hold theirs.
Tell a family member which topics about your body or health are off the table.
Ask for the meeting agenda before you agree to attend.
Say "I am done for today" out loud at the end of your work and close every tab.
Catch yourself agreeing just to end a conversation today, and go back to say what you meant.
Say "I am not going to answer that" to one question that oversteps, and change the subject.
Write the word "no" on a sticky note and keep it where you take calls, as a reminder that it is an option.
Tell a friend who wants to vent that you can listen tonight but not right now.
Decline a video call and offer a phone call or a text instead, if that is what you have energy for.
Notice when you say "it's fine" today and check whether it is actually fine.
Ask a coworker to book time on your calendar instead of stopping by your desk.
Practice saying "I need to go" and then actually leaving, rather than lingering by the door.
Choose one afternoon this week that is off limits for errands for other people.
Tell a parent or older relative that you love them and you will not be discussing that topic.
Say "I am going to keep my weekend free" when someone asks what you are doing, and keep it free.
Write down the last request that made your stomach drop, and what you wish you had said.
Refuse to read a message that arrives during your one protected hour today.
Let the doorbell or a delivery wait a few minutes if you are in the middle of something that matters to you.
Ask a friend to stop teasing you about one thing, in a plain sentence, without laughing it off.
Tell your team you will not be reachable during your lunch break from now on.
Say "That is more than I can offer" to a request for time, money, or effort that goes past your limit.
Notice a compliment that comes with a request attached and answer only the request.
Decide which family visits you will drive to this season and which you will not.
Write a boundary about your evenings in one sentence and read it before you say yes to anything tonight.
Turn off the read receipts on your messages so no one can time your replies.
Tell a friend you are leaving the party before you feel exhausted, not after.
Say "I am not taking on anything new this week" to the first person who asks.
Ask someone to lower their voice when they raise it at you, and pause until they do.
Practice a boundary on a walk: rehearse the sentence, hear how it sounds, adjust the words.
Refuse to pick up a shift on your day off without offering an excuse.
Notice one time today when you laughed to smooth over a comment that stung, and let the silence sit instead.
Tell someone who keeps borrowing your things that you would like them to ask each time.
Write down which holidays or celebrations you will host this year and which you will only attend.
Say "I am going to sit this one out" to a group decision that does not need you.
Decline to give your phone number to someone you do not want to hear from.
Ask a coworker to stop calling you their backup for a job that is not yours.
Set a limit on how long you will spend helping with someone's homework or project tonight.
Tell your partner what kind of support you want when you are upset: listening, advice, or space.
Write down who tends to bring the most requests into your week, and one thing you will decline from them.
Say "I do not do that anymore" about one task you have quietly retired from, and watch nothing fall apart.
Notice the urge to send a second explanatory message after a no, and do not send it.
Take a full day off from replying in a group chat and say so if anyone asks.
Ask for a raise, a fee, or a fair split for work you have been doing for free.
Tell a friend who asks for a ride at the last minute that you need more notice.
Say what time you will be home tonight, and be home then.
Practice the phrase "I am not the right audience for that" when someone shares something you did not ask to hear.
Decline a joint gift, a shared plan, or a group purchase you do not want to fund.
Write down one thing you would say if you were not afraid of being called selfish.
Set a boundary with a screen: choose the hour tonight when the television or laptop goes off.
Tell a coworker you will not cover for a mistake that is not yours.
Notice when you pre-apologize before asking for something today, and ask without it.
Say "Please do not comment on my food" or "on my body" to someone who does, once, calmly.
Ask a family member to give you some warning before big news or hard conversations.
Refuse to check in on someone's mood every hour and let them come to you if they need something.
Write one sentence for what you will do if a boundary is ignored twice, and keep it where you can find it.
Say "I am going to hang up now" if a call turns into something you did not agree to.
Tell a relative that you are not able to host this year, and offer nothing else.
Decide on one purchase you will not make for someone who could make it themselves.
Notice how often you say "just" before a request today, and drop it once: "Can you take this?"
Ask your household to let you finish a meal before bringing you problems.
Practice saying "I will stop there" at the end of an explanation, and stop.
Tell a friend you would rather do a short walk than a long dinner, and let them decide if they are in.
Say no to a meeting with no agenda or end time.
Write down a rule for weekends that protects one morning, and tell whoever needs to know.
Decline to be the one who always sends the reminders, and let something be forgotten.
Ask a colleague to raise the issue with the person it concerns, rather than through you.
Notice when someone tells you how you feel today and correct them gently: "Actually, I feel..."
Turn down a request for help moving, painting, or hauling if your body needs the rest.
Tell someone who reads your screen over your shoulder that you would like some privacy.
Say "I want to be asked, not told" to one person who tends to assign you things.
Recall a time you held a boundary and someone was fine with it. Write it down, and keep that memory nearby.
Refuse to keep a secret you were never asked whether you were willing to keep.
Set a limit on how many times you will reread a message before responding, and stick to it.
Ask for a quiet hour on a Sunday morning and take it, even if the house is full.
Tell a friend who shares your news with others that you would like them to check with you first.
Say "I have already answered that" when someone asks the same thing a third time, and do not answer again.
Write down what "being nice" has cost you this month, in hours or in sleep.
Tell a coworker who eats at your desk, uses your mug, or borrows your charger that you would like them to ask.
Decline a conversation about politics, religion, or money at a gathering by saying "Let's talk about something else."
Spot a moment today when you waited for permission you did not need, and act without it.
Ask a friend who always needs a favor what they can offer in return this time.
Practice saying "I need more time" instead of rushing to meet a deadline that was never realistic.
Choose one evening this week for yourself and mark it on the shared calendar so no one books over it.
Tell your family that you will leave the room if voices get raised, then follow through.
Say "I am going to trust my own read on this" when someone insists you are overreacting.
Refuse to answer work messages while you are at a child's game, a doctor's office, or a funeral.
Write a boundary for the next family trip: what you will pay for, what you will not, and share it before you go.
Let someone be annoyed with you for a whole afternoon without trying to fix it.
Ask a friend to stop sending you articles about how to fix your life.
Tell a colleague that you do not discuss salary, dating, or health at work, and mean whichever one is true.
Say "I need to check with myself first" to a request, out loud, and see how it lands.
Notice how your shoulders feel when you receive a request today, and let that inform your answer.
Decide which coworkers can text your personal phone and tell the rest to use email.
Write down what you were taught about saying no as a child, and whether you still believe it.
Turn down a sales pitch, a survey, or a petition on the street with a nod and keep walking.
Tell a friend you will not be the go-between in their conflict with someone else.
Say "That sounds hard, and I am not able to help with it" to one problem that is not yours.
Ask the people you live with for one hour of no questions after you get home.
Practice a boundary in a store: decline the extended warranty, the rewards card, or the upsell without explaining.
Refuse to cancel your plans because someone else changed theirs.
Catch a moment today when you predicted anger from someone, and check whether it actually came.
Tell a family member that you will visit for two hours, not the whole day.
List one thing you agreed to on autopilot this week and undo it if you still can.
Say no to reviewing, proofreading, or editing someone's work tonight if your own is not done.
Decline a friend's request to borrow your car, and offer no substitute.
Ask a coworker to stop making jokes about your accent, your age, or your background, plainly and once.
Set a specific number of times you will say yes to extra work this month, and count.
Tell your partner that you would like to make one decision this week without discussing it first.
State "I am not going to change my mind on this" and then change the subject.
Notice a request that is really a demand in disguise, and treat it as a request anyway.
Write a message declining a wedding, reunion, or big event you do not want to attend, and send it.
Refuse to answer the phone during dinner, even from someone who calls often.
Ask a friend who tends to cancel to confirm the morning of, so you can plan around it.
Tell a manager that you can take on the new project if something else comes off your plate, and name it.
Say "That is not a conversation for right now" and set a time when it would be.
Practice giving a one-word answer today when a longer one is not owed: "No." "Later." "Maybe."
Decline a request for a reference, a recommendation, or an introduction you do not feel good about.
Notice when you agree to something only because everyone else did, and speak up.
Tell someone who shares your photos online that you would like to be asked first.
Write down the boundary you will hold at your next family gathering, and reread it in the car.

title: Living by Your Values
description: For when your days are full but do not feel like yours. Each day asks you to notice what matters to you and take one small action in that direction, so your life lines up a little more with what you care about.
tasks: Write down five words that describe the person you want to be.
Pick one of your values and do one small thing today that expresses it.
Think of a person you admire and write down which of their qualities you want more of.
Notice one moment today when you acted in line with what you care about. Name the value.
Write down one thing you spend time on that does not match your values, and one small change.
Ask yourself: "If today were a chapter, what would I want it to be about?" Then live one page of it.
Do something today for a cause, a person, or a place you care about.
Choose one value and put it somewhere you will see it all day.
Write down what you would want a friend to say about you at your eightieth birthday.
Make one decision today based on what matters, not on what is easiest.
Spend fifteen minutes on something that feels meaningful rather than urgent.
List three moments in your life when you felt most yourself. What did they have in common?
Say what you think today in one conversation where you would normally keep quiet.
Notice one value you have been neglecting and give it ten minutes today.
Write a sentence that starts with "I want to be the kind of person who..."
Pick one relationship and do one thing that reflects how much it matters to you.
Spend money, even a little, on something that matches your values instead of a habit.
Notice when you feel proud today and write down what value you were honoring.
Do one thing today that your younger self would be glad to see you doing.
Write down one value you hold that you rarely talk about, and tell someone about it.
Turn one value into a tiny daily action: "kindness" becomes "one warm message a day."
Choose how you want to show up in one meeting or gathering today, and do it on purpose.
Notice one thing you do out of habit, and ask whether it reflects who you want to be.
Write down one value you got from your family and whether you want to keep it.
Do a small act of courage today in the direction of something you care about.
Spend ten minutes learning about something you value, a skill, a place, a cause.
Write down what "a good day" looks like for you, in three lines.
Let one value guide how you treat yourself today, not just others.
Notice a moment today when you were pulled away from your values, and gently return.
Look back over this challenge and write down the two or three values that came up most. Those are yours.
Name the value behind your morning routine, then adjust one small part of it to match that value better.
Before you open your phone this morning, say out loud one thing you want your day to stand for.
Look at your calendar for the week and circle the one commitment that matters most to you. Protect it.
Write down a value you admire in a coworker and find one way to bring it into your own work today.
Cancel or shorten one thing today that you agreed to only out of obligation, and use the time on something you care about.
Take a ten-minute walk and ask yourself what you would do with your time if no one were watching.
Choose a book, podcast, or article that speaks to something you care about and give it twenty minutes tonight.
Pick a value and write three ways you could express it at work, then try the smallest one before lunch.
Text a friend and ask what they think you care most about. Compare their answer with your own.
Notice which of your values shows up in how you handle money this week, and write it down.
Cook or order a meal that reflects something you believe in, whether that is health, community, or the local farm.
Write a short note to yourself about why your job matters, beyond the paycheck, and keep it in your wallet.
Say no to one request today so that you can say yes to something that matters more.
Rank your top five values from most to least lived this month, then give the last one twenty minutes.
Ask an older relative or friend what they wish they had spent more time on, and sit with the answer.
Pick one object in your home that represents a value you hold. Move it somewhere you will see it more.
Spend your lunch break doing one thing that lines up with what you care about rather than scrolling.
Write down a decision you are avoiding, then list which of your values each option honors.
Set a timer for five minutes and list everything you did yesterday that felt like it was truly yours.
Pick one value and let it choose your evening plan tonight.
Catch yourself saying yes on autopilot today. Ask what you would have chosen on purpose.
Write a one-line mission statement for the next week and read it before you start work.
Look at how you spent money in the last seven days and mark each purchase with the value it served, if any.
Clean or organize one small space in a way that reflects how you want to live, not how you have been living.
Choose one small daily habit and connect it to a value in writing: "I make my bed because I value calm."
Reach out to someone who shares a value with you and suggest doing something about it together.
Write down one thing you want to be remembered for, then do a five-minute version of it today.
When envy shows up today, ask what value it is pointing to, and take one step toward it.
Sit outside for ten minutes and ask what kind of life you want to build. Write down the first honest answer.
Pick a value you hold about the environment and change one household habit today to match it.
Decide what "enough" looks like for you in one area of life, and write it down where you will see it.
Do the task you have been putting off that matters most to you, even if only for fifteen minutes.
Practice listening in one conversation today the way a person you admire listens.
Ask yourself what you would want your work to be about if the title did not matter, then do one hour of that.

Choose a value to lead with in your next hard conversation, and plan one sentence that expresses it.
Spend twenty minutes on a hobby you dropped because it felt unproductive, and notice what it gives you.
Notice one place where you spend energy pleasing others, and reclaim ten minutes of it for what you value.
Write down what you believe about rest, then take a break today that matches that belief.
Pick a value and photograph one thing today that represents it.

Choose one meeting today to speak from your values rather than from what will be popular.
Give ten minutes this evening to a creative project that means something to you, with no goal of finishing.
Plan one small adventure for the coming month that reflects your curiosity, and take the first step to book it.

Practice saying "That matters to me" once today in a conversation where you would usually stay vague.
Write down one boundary you want to hold this week and the value it protects.
Spend an hour offline this evening on something that would make your future self grateful.

Set aside thirty minutes this weekend for the one activity that makes you feel most like yourself.
Answer this in writing: what do you want your home to feel like to a guest? Change one small thing toward that.

Practice patience in one line, one traffic jam, or one slow conversation today because it reflects who you want to be.

Take one step, however small, toward a long-held goal that you have been calling "someday."

Spend the first ten minutes of your workday on the task that matters most, before email pulls you elsewhere.

Take a fifteen-minute walk after dinner and ask what your life would look like if you fully trusted your own values.

Let one of your values pick what you read, watch, or listen to tonight.

title: Small Acts of Kindness
description: A daily practice of doing something small for someone else, which has a way of lifting the giver too. Each day is one easy, specific act of kindness, most of them taking less than five minutes.

title: Meeting Anger Early
description: For anger that arrives fast and leaves a mess behind. Each day gives you one way to notice it sooner, cool it a little, and say what you mean without the heat, one practice at a time.
tasks: Write down the last three things that made you angry. Look for what they have in common.
Notice where anger shows up in your body first today: jaw, chest, hands, stomach.
When you feel a flash of anger, breathe out slowly for a count of six before you say anything.
Practice the phrase "I need a minute" and use it once today if you need it.
Write down what you were really feeling underneath your last angry moment. Hurt? Scared? Tired?
Unclench your hands and jaw on purpose five times today.
Take a ten-minute walk when something irritates you, before responding.
Say "I feel frustrated when..." instead of "You always..." once today.
Rate your anger from zero to ten when you notice it. Respond only when it is under five.
Splash cold water on your face or hold something cold when your temper rises.
Write down what you would want to say in the heat of the moment. Then wait an hour and reread it.
Notice one small annoyance today and let it go without commenting.
Ask yourself, "What do I need right now?" when you feel angry, and try to give it to yourself.
Move your body hard for two minutes, stairs, a fast walk, when anger builds.
Get enough to eat and drink today. Hunger and thirst make everything sharper.
Write a list of your early warning signs of anger and keep it on your phone.
Delay one reaction by ten minutes today and see if the same response still feels right.
Say sorry for something small today, cleanly, without explaining why you did it.
Notice one thought that fuels your anger, like "they did that on purpose," and write down another possibility.
Tell someone calmly what you would like them to do differently, in one sentence.
Take three slow breaths before you open a message or email that might annoy you.
Spend ten minutes doing something physical and productive, cleaning, chopping, digging, when tension builds.
Write down what anger has cost you recently and what it has protected.

title: Rebuilding Confidence in Small Steps
description: For when your confidence has taken a knock and everything feels like a risk. Each day is one small, doable act of showing up, so evidence that you can builds one day at a time.
tasks: Write down three things you have done in your life that were hard at the time and that you managed.
Speak first in one conversation today.
Stand up straight, shoulders back, for one minute and notice how it changes your mood.
Ask a question in a meeting, a class, or a shop today.
Write down one skill you are good at and one piece of evidence for it.
Wear something today that makes you feel like yourself.
Say your opinion once today without adding "but I might be wrong."
Make one small decision quickly today and do not revisit it.
Introduce yourself to someone new.
Set a tiny goal for today and finish it. Write "done" next to it.
Accept a compliment with only "thank you."
Try something you are not good at yet for ten minutes, just to practice being a beginner.
Write down what a confident version of you would do today. Do one part of it.
Make a phone call you have been avoiding.
Look someone in the eye when you say hello today.
Write down one thing you did well this week that nobody noticed.
Volunteer for one small thing, a task, an errand, a turn, before you have time to talk yourself out of it.
Practice saying "I don't know, but I can find out."
Do one thing today that scares you a little, on a scale of one to ten a three or a four.
Write down the worst-case outcome of something you are avoiding, then how you would handle it.
Notice one time today you compared yourself to someone and turn your attention back to your own next step.
Ask for help with something today. Confident people do.
Teach someone something small that you know.
Sit at the front, or in the middle, instead of the back.
Write down one thing you believe about yourself that is out of date.
Speak a little slower and a little louder than usual in one conversation today.
